problems.title: Inscribed angle intercepting a known arc
problems.question:
In the diagram, points $A$, $B$, and $C$ lie on circle $O$. Arc $AC$ (not containing $B$) measures $134°$. Find $m\angle ABC$.

$\textbf{(A)}\ 268° \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 134° \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 46° \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 67°$
problems.figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-3.1000 -3.1000 6.2000 6.2000" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Geometry figure"><g transform="scale(1,-1)"><circle cx="0" cy="0" r="2.5000" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.04"/><line x1="1.6070" y1="-1.9151" x2="-2.3492" y2="-0.8551" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.04"/><line x1="1.6070" y1="-1.9151" x2="1.0168" y2="2.2839" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.04"/><circle cx="0" cy="0" r="0.0375" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="-2.3492" cy="-0.8551" r="0.0375" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="1.0168" cy="2.2839" r="0.0375" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="1.6070" cy="-1.9151" r="0.0375" fill="currentColor"/></g><text x="0.0000" y="0.0000" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="0.2800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="currentColor" dx="0.1500" dy="0.2500">O</text><text x="-2.5560" y="0.9303" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="0.2800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="currentColor">A</text><text x="1.1063" y="-2.4848" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="0.2800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="currentColor">C</text><text x="1.7484" y="2.0836" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="0.2800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="currentColor">B</text></svg>

solutionSteps.title: Identify the Inscribed Angle
solutionSteps.description: Angle $ABC$ is an **inscribed angle** because its vertex $B$ lies on the circle and its two sides ($BA$ and $BC$) are chords of the circle. The intercepted arc is arc $AC$ not containing $B$, which measures $134°$.

solutionSteps.title: Apply the Inscribed Angle Theorem
solutionSteps.description:
The **Inscribed Angle Theorem** states that an inscribed angle equals **half** the measure of its intercepted arc:
$$m\angle ABC = \frac{1}{2} \cdot m\overset{\frown}{AC}$$
$$m\angle ABC = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 134° = 67°$$

solutionSteps.title: Eliminate the Distractors
solutionSteps.description:
• **(A) 268°** — This is the major arc $AC$ (containing $B$): $360° - 134° = 226°$... actually a common error is doubling instead of halving: $134° \times 2 = 268°$. Wrong direction.
• **(B) 134°** — This mistakes the inscribed angle for the arc itself, forgetting to halve. A central angle would equal the arc, but an inscribed angle does not.
• **(C) 46°** — This is $\frac{1}{2}(90° - 67°)$ or a subtraction error; some students subtract from 90°: $90° - 46° = 44°$. Reflects confusion with complementary relationships.
• **(D) 67°** ✓ — Correctly applies the Inscribed Angle Theorem: $\frac{1}{2}(134°) = 67°$.

solutionSteps.title: State the Answer
solutionSteps.description: The correct answer is $\textbf{(D)}\ 67°$.

verdict.rederivation: Inscribed Angle Theorem: ∠ABC = ½ · arc AC = ½(134°) = 67°. The distractors — 134 (forgot to halve), 46, 113 (180−67) — are all plausible misconceptions. Figure renders faithfully.

problems.title: Inscribed angle from intercepted arc
problems.question: In the diagram, points $A$, $B$, and $C$ lie on circle $O$. Arc $AC$ (not containing $B$) measures $arc\,AC = (6x + 4)°$, and the inscribed angle $\angle ABC = (2x + 15)°$. Set up and solve an equation to find $m\angle ABC$.
problems.figureSvg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-3.1000 -3.1000 6.2000 6.2000" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Geometry figure"><g transform="scale(1,-1)"><circle cx="0" cy="0" r="2.5000" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.04"/><line x1="-2.3492" y1="-0.8551" x2="0.0000" y2="2.5000" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.04"/><line x1="0.0000" y1="2.5000" x2="2.3492" y2="-0.8551" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.04"/><circle cx="0" cy="0" r="0.0375" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="-2.3492" cy="-0.8551" r="0.0375" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="0.0000" cy="2.5000" r="0.0375" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="2.3492" cy="-0.8551" r="0.0375" fill="currentColor"/></g><text x="0.0000" y="0.0000" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="0.2800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="currentColor" dx="0.1500" dy="0.2500">O</text><text x="-2.5560" y="0.9303" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="0.2800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="currentColor">A</text><text x="0.0000" y="-2.7200" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="0.2800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="currentColor">B</text><text x="2.5560" y="0.9303" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="0.2800" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" fill="currentColor">C</text></svg>

solutionSteps.title: Understand the Setup
solutionSteps.description:
We have three points $A$, $B$, $C$ on circle $O$. The **inscribed angle** $\angle ABC$ has its vertex on the circle and its two sides are chords that cut off arc $AC$ (the arc not containing $B$). That arc is the **intercepted arc** for this angle.

The key relationship to use: the **Inscribed Angle Theorem** says an inscribed angle equals exactly **half** its intercepted arc. Written as a formula:
$$\angle ABC = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \overset{\frown}{AC}$$
This immediately lets us set up one equation in one unknown $x$.

solutionSteps.title: Set Up the Equation
solutionSteps.description:
Substitute the given expressions into the Inscribed Angle Theorem:
$$\underbrace{(2x + 15)}_{\angle ABC} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \underbrace{(6x + 4)}_{\overset{\frown}{AC}}$$
Multiply both sides by $2$ to clear the fraction:
$$2(2x + 15) = 6x + 4$$
$$4x + 30 = 6x + 4$$

solutionSteps.title: Solve for $x$
solutionSteps.description:
Collect the $x$-terms on one side and constants on the other:
$$30 - 4 = 6x - 4x$$
$$26 = 2x$$
$$x = 13$$

solutionSteps.title: Find $m\angle ABC$
solutionSteps.description:
Substitute $x = 13$ back into the expression for the inscribed angle:
$$m\angle ABC = 2(13) + 15 = 26 + 15 = 41°$$

**Quick check:** Arc $AC = 6(13) + 4 = 82°$, and $\frac{1}{2}(82°) = 41°$ ✓

verdict.rederivation: Inscribed angle with algebra: arc AC = (6x+4)°, ∠ABC = (2x+15)°; set 2x+15 = ½(6x+4) → x = 13 → ∠ABC = 41°. Figure renders faithfully.

problems.title: Optimization — minimum cost for open-top box
problems.question: A company needs to manufacture an open-top rectangular box with a square base. The box must have a volume of exactly 32,000 cm³. The material for the base costs $0.08 per cm², and the material for the four sides costs $0.05 per cm². What side length (in cm) of the square base minimizes the total material cost of the box? Express your answer as a decimal to 3 significant figures.

solutionSteps.title: Understand the Problem
solutionSteps.description:
We have an open-top box with a **square base** of side $x$ and height $h$. Two constraints drive the math:

1. **Volume** is fixed: $x^2 h = 32{,}000$
2. **Cost** depends on area — base costs more per cm² than the sides.

The key insight: volume ties $h$ to $x$, so we can eliminate $h$ and write cost as a **single-variable function** of $x$. Then minimizing is just setting the derivative to zero.

**Watch for:** a term that grows with $x$ (base area) fighting a term that shrinks with $x$ (side area, because taller boxes get cheaper bases). The minimum sits where these forces balance.

solutionSteps.title: Express h via Volume
solutionSteps.description:
From $x^2 h = 32{,}000$, solve for $h$:
$$h = \frac{32{,}000}{x^2}$$
Every quantity in the cost function will now be written purely in terms of $x$.

solutionSteps.title: Build the Cost Function
solutionSteps.description:
**Base** (one square, area $x^2$, rate $\$0.08$):
$$C_{\text{base}} = 0.08x^2$$

**Four sides** (each rectangle $x \times h$, rate $\$0.05$):
$$C_{\text{sides}} = 0.05 \times 4xh = 0.20 \cdot x \cdot \frac{32{,}000}{x^2} = \frac{6{,}400}{x}$$

Total cost:
$$C(x) = 0.08x^2 + \frac{6{,}400}{x}$$

The first term grows as $x$ increases (bigger base), the second shrinks (shorter, cheaper sides). The minimum is somewhere in between.

solutionSteps.title: Solve for x
solutionSteps.description:
$$x = \sqrt[3]{40{,}000}$$

Factor to simplify: $40{,}000 = 8 \times 5{,}000 = 8 \times 5 \times 1{,}000$, so
$$x = 2\sqrt[3]{5{,}000} = 2 \times 10\sqrt[3]{5} = 20\sqrt[3]{5}$$

Numerically: $\sqrt[3]{5} \approx 1.70998$, giving
$$x = 20 \times 1.70998 \approx 34.1995\ldots \text{ cm}$$

To 3 significant figures: $x \approx \mathbf{34.2}$ **cm**.

solutionSteps.title: Confirm It's a Minimum
solutionSteps.description:
The second derivative confirms this is a **minimum**, not a maximum:
$$C''(x) = 0.16 + \frac{12{,}800}{x^3}$$

Since both terms are strictly positive for all $x > 0$, we have $C''(x) > 0$ everywhere — the cost curve is **concave up**, so $x = 20\sqrt[3]{5}$ is indeed a global minimum.

verdict.rederivation: Cost C = 0.08x² + 6400/x; C′ = 0.16x − 6400/x² = 0 → x³ = 40000 → x = 20∛5 ≈ 34.2 cm. Distractors capture common slips.

problems.title: Related rates — sliding ladder on a wall
problems.question: A 13-meter ladder leans against a vertical wall. The base of the ladder is being pulled away from the wall at a constant rate of 0.5 m/s. At the instant when the base of the ladder is 5 meters from the wall, how fast (in m/s) is the top of the ladder sliding down the wall? Express your answer as a decimal to 3 significant figures.

solutionSteps.title: Understand the Problem
solutionSteps.description:
We have a 13 m ladder leaning against a wall. The base slides away from the wall at $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0.5$ m/s, and we want $\frac{dy}{dt}$ — how fast the top slides **down** — when the base is $x = 5$ m from the wall.

The ladder's length never changes, so the horizontal distance $x$ and vertical height $y$ are always connected by the **Pythagorean theorem**: $$x^2 + y^2 = 13^2$$
This is our key equation. Differentiating it with respect to time links the rates $\frac{dx}{dt}$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}$ together.

solutionSteps.title: Find y at the Instant
solutionSteps.description:
At the instant when $x = 5$ m, plug into the Pythagorean equation to find the height $y$: $$5^2 + y^2 = 13^2$$ $$25 + y^2 = 169$$ $$y^2 = 144 \implies y = 12 \text{ m}$$
Notice the **5–12–13 right triangle** — a classic Pythagorean triple that makes the arithmetic clean.

solutionSteps.title: Differentiate with Respect to Time
solutionSteps.description:
Differentiate both sides of $x^2 + y^2 = 169$ with respect to time $t$. The constant 169 vanishes, and the **chain rule** gives a rate on each variable: $$2x\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$$
Dividing through by 2: $$x\frac{dx}{dt} + y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$$
This equation says: as $x$ grows, $y$ must shrink at exactly the compensating rate to keep the ladder length fixed.

solutionSteps.title: Solve for dy/dt
solutionSteps.description:
Isolate $\frac{dy}{dt}$: $$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{x}{y}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}$$
Substitute $x = 5$, $y = 12$, $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0.5$: $$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{5}{12} \times 0.5 = -\frac{2.5}{12} \approx -0.20833\ldots \text{ m/s}$$
The **negative sign** confirms the top is moving **downward**. The speed of descent is $|\frac{dy}{dt}| \approx 0.208$ m/s.

problems.finalAnswer:
$\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -\dfrac{5}{24} \approx -0.208 \text{ m/s}$

The top of the ladder slides **down** the wall at $0.208$ m/s.

verdict.rederivation: 5-12-13 right triangle; differentiating x²+y²=169 gives dy/dt = −(x/y)·dx/dt = −(5/12)(0.5) = −0.208 m/s — the ladder's top descends at 0.208 m/s.

problems.title: Minimum fence cost — optimization
problems.question:
A rancher plans to build a rectangular holding pen along the straight bank of a river (so no fence is needed on the river side). The pen must enclose an area of $1{,}800$ m². Fencing for the two sides perpendicular to the river costs $\$12$ per meter, and fencing for the single side parallel to the river (opposite the bank) costs $\$8$ per meter.

**(a)** Define variables for the dimensions of the pen and write the objective function (total cost) together with the constraint.

**(b)** Express the cost as a function of a single variable and find its critical point(s).

**(c)** Use the first or second derivative test to confirm that the critical point is a minimum, and state the dimensions and minimum cost, rounded to 3 significant figures.

solutionSteps.title: Understand the Setup
solutionSteps.description:
We have a rectangle bordered by a river on one side. The river side needs no fence, so we pay for:
- **Two sides** perpendicular to the river (the "widths") at $\$12$/m each
- **One side** parallel to the river (the "length") at $\$8$/m

The key insight for optimization problems like this: write cost in terms of **two** variables, then use the area constraint to eliminate one, leaving a single-variable function we can minimize with calculus. Watch for the asymmetric cost structure — the two sides share a rate while the one parallel side has its own rate.

solutionSteps.title: Part (a): Variables, Constraint & Objective
solutionSteps.description:
Let:
- $x$ = the length of each side **perpendicular** to the river (m)
- $y$ = the length of the side **parallel** to the river (m)

**Constraint** (area must be 1,800 m²):
$$xy = 1800$$

**Objective function** (total fencing cost):
$$C = 2(12)x + 8y = 24x + 8y$$
The factor of 2 appears because there are two perpendicular sides.

solutionSteps.title: Part (b): Single-Variable Cost Function
solutionSteps.description:
Solve the constraint for $y$:
$$y = \frac{1800}{x}$$

Substitute into $C$:
$$C(x) = 24x + 8 \cdot \frac{1800}{x} = 24x + \frac{14{,}400}{x}$$

This is valid for $x > 0$. Now find the critical point by setting $C'(x) = 0$:
$$C'(x) = 24 - \frac{14{,}400}{x^2} = 0$$
$$x^2 = \frac{14{,}400}{24} = 600$$
$$\boxed{x = \sqrt{600} = 10\sqrt{6} \approx 24.5 \text{ m}}$$

This is the only critical point on $(0, \infty)$.

solutionSteps.title: Part (c): Confirm Minimum & State Answer
solutionSteps.description:
**Second Derivative Test:**
$$C''(x) = \frac{28{,}800}{x^3}$$

Since $x > 0$, we have $C''(x) > 0$ for all valid $x$, so $C(x)$ is **concave up** everywhere — confirming the critical point is a **global minimum**.

**Dimensions:**
$$x = 10\sqrt{6} \approx 24.5 \text{ m (perpendicular sides)}$$
$$y = \frac{1800}{10\sqrt{6}} = 30\sqrt{6} \approx 73.5 \text{ m (parallel side)}$$

Notice that $y = 3x$: the optimal parallel side is exactly 3 times the perpendicular side — a clean ratio that reflects how the costs balance out.

**Minimum Cost:**
$$C = 24(10\sqrt{6}) + \frac{14{,}400}{10\sqrt{6}} = 240\sqrt{6} + 240\sqrt{6} = 480\sqrt{6} \approx \$1{,}180$$

At the optimum, cost splits **evenly** between the perpendicular sides and the parallel side — a hallmark of well-structured optimization problems.

verdict.rederivation: Minimize C = 24x + 14400/x → C′ = 24 − 14400/x² = 0 → x = 10√6, y = 30√6 → C = 480√6 ≈ $1180. An excellent optimization problem for the level.

problems.title: Expanding ripple — related rates
problems.question:
A stone is dropped into a calm lake, producing a circular ripple whose radius expands at a constant rate of $3.5$ cm/s.

**(a)** Define all relevant variables and state the equation relating them.

**(b)** Differentiate your equation with respect to time.

**(c)** At the instant the radius is $12$ cm, how fast is the area of the circular ripple increasing? Express your answer in cm²/s, rounded to 3 significant figures.

solutionSteps.title: Understand the Problem
solutionSteps.description:
A circular ripple grows outward over time. We know **how fast the radius is growing** and want to find **how fast the area is growing** at a specific moment.

This is a **related rates** problem — two quantities (radius $r$ and area $A$) both change with time, and their rates of change are linked through the formula for the area of a circle. The key insight: differentiate that area formula with respect to time $t$ to connect $\frac{dr}{dt}$ (given) to $\frac{dA}{dt}$ (what we want).

solutionSteps.title: Part (a): Define Variables
solutionSteps.description:
Let:
- $t$ = time (seconds)
- $r = r(t)$ = radius of the ripple at time $t$ (cm)
- $A = A(t)$ = area of the ripple at time $t$ (cm²)

The equation relating them is the area of a circle:
$$A = \pi r^2$$

The known rate is $\dfrac{dr}{dt} = 3.5$ cm/s.

solutionSteps.title: Part (b): Differentiate with Respect to Time
solutionSteps.description:
Differentiate both sides of $A = \pi r^2$ with respect to $t$, using the **Chain Rule** on the right side (since $r$ is itself a function of $t$):
$$\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r \cdot \frac{dr}{dt}$$

This equation says: the rate of area growth equals $2\pi r$ times the rate of radius growth. The faster the radius grows *or* the larger $r$ already is, the faster the area expands.

solutionSteps.title: Part (c): Substitute Known Values
solutionSteps.description:
At the instant $r = 12$ cm, substitute $r = 12$ and $\dfrac{dr}{dt} = 3.5$ into the differentiated equation:
$$\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi (12)(3.5) = 84\pi$$

Evaluating numerically:
$$\frac{dA}{dt} = 84\pi \approx 263.893\ldots \approx \mathbf{264} \text{ cm}^2\text{/s}$$

verdict.rederivation: Related rates on area: dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt = 2π(12)(3.5) = 84π ≈ 264 cm²/s. Clean and direct.

problems.title: Sliding ladder — related rates and optimization
problems.question:
A 10-meter ladder leans against a vertical wall. The base of the ladder slides away from the wall at a rate of $0.4$ m/s.

**(a)** Define variables for the horizontal distance from the wall to the base of the ladder and the vertical height of the top of the ladder. Write the equation relating them.

**(b)** Differentiate with respect to time and find the rate at which the top of the ladder is sliding down the wall at the instant the base is $6$ m from the wall. Express your answer in m/s, rounded to 3 significant figures.

**(c)** The area of the triangle formed by the ladder, wall, and ground is $A = \frac{1}{2}xy$, where $x$ is the base distance and $y$ is the wall height. Using your expressions for $x$, $y$, and their rates from parts (a) and (b), find $\frac{dA}{dt}$ at the instant the base is $6$ m from the wall. Then, treating $x$ as the independent variable (with $x$ ranging over $(0, 10)$), determine the value of $x$ at which the area $A(x)$ is maximized and confirm it is a maximum. State both the rate $\frac{dA}{dt}$ at $x = 6$ m and the maximum area, each rounded to 3 significant figures.

solutionSteps.title: Understand the Setup
solutionSteps.description:
We have a 10 m ladder, a vertical wall, and the ground forming a right triangle. The ladder is the hypotenuse (always length 10 m), the ground leg grows as the base slides out, and the wall leg shrinks as the top slides down.

The key insight: **the ladder length is constant**, which is what links the horizontal and vertical changes. We'll use the Pythagorean theorem to write that constraint, then differentiate it with respect to time — a technique called **related rates** — to connect the rates of change.

solutionSteps.title: Define Variables & Equation
solutionSteps.description:
Let:
- $x$ = horizontal distance (m) from the wall to the base of the ladder
- $y$ = vertical height (m) of the top of the ladder on the wall
- $t$ = time (s)

Both $x$ and $y$ are **functions of time**. The ladder's fixed length gives the constraint:

$$x^2 + y^2 = 10^2 = 100$$

This is the equation relating $x$ and $y$ at every instant.

solutionSteps.title: Differentiate with Respect to Time
solutionSteps.description:
Differentiate both sides of $x^2 + y^2 = 100$ with respect to $t$, using the **chain rule** on each term (since both $x$ and $y$ depend on $t$):

$$2x\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$$

Divide through by 2 and isolate $\frac{dy}{dt}$:

$$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{x}{y}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}$$

The negative sign confirms that as $x$ **increases** (base slides out), $y$ **decreases** (top slides down) — physically correct.

solutionSteps.title: Find y at x = 6 m
solutionSteps.description:
Substitute $x = 6$ into the Pythagorean constraint to find the corresponding wall height:

$$y = \sqrt{100 - 6^2} = \sqrt{100 - 36} = \sqrt{64} = 8 \text{ m}$$

So at this instant: $x = 6$ m, $y = 8$ m — a classic 6-8-10 right triangle (a scaled 3-4-5).

solutionSteps.title: Compute dy/dt at x = 6 m
solutionSteps.description:
We know $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0.4$ m/s, $x = 6$ m, $y = 8$ m. Substitute:

$$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{x}{y}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt} = -\frac{6}{8}\times 0.4 = -\frac{2.4}{8} = -0.3 \text{ m/s}$$

The top of the ladder is sliding **down** at $\mathbf{0.300}$ **m/s** when the base is 6 m from the wall.

solutionSteps.title: Find dA/dt at x = 6 m
solutionSteps.description:
The triangle's area is $A = \frac{1}{2}xy$. Differentiate with respect to $t$ using the **product rule**:

$$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\cdot y + x\cdot\frac{dy}{dt}\right)$$

Substitute all known values ($x=6$, $y=8$, $\frac{dx}{dt}=0.4$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=-0.3$):

$$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\bigl((0.4)(8) + (6)(-0.3)\bigr) = \frac{1}{2}(3.2 - 1.8) = \frac{1.4}{2} = \mathbf{0.700 \text{ m}^2\text{/s}}$$

At this instant the triangle's area is **growing** — the base is expanding faster than the height is shrinking.

solutionSteps.title: Maximize A(x) Over (0, 10)
solutionSteps.description:
Express $A$ purely as a function of $x$ by substituting $y = \sqrt{100 - x^2}$:

$$A(x) = \frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{100 - x^2}, \quad x \in (0, 10)$$

Differentiate and set $A'(x) = 0$. Using the product rule:

$$A'(x) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{100 - 2x^2}{\sqrt{100-x^2}}$$

The numerator is what can equal zero (the denominator is always positive on the open interval):

$$100 - 2x^2 = 0 \implies x^2 = 50 \implies x = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07 \text{ m}$$

**Confirming it's a maximum:** $A'(x) > 0$ for $x < 5\sqrt{2}$ and $A'(x) < 0$ for $x > 5\sqrt{2}$, so this is a genuine **global maximum** on $(0,10)$.

At $x = 5\sqrt{2}$, the corresponding height is:
$$y = \sqrt{100 - 50} = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$$

Note that $x = y = 5\sqrt{2}$: **the area is maximized when the triangle is isosceles** (base = height), a clean geometric insight.

The maximum area:
$$A_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}(5\sqrt{2})(5\sqrt{2}) = \frac{1}{2}\times 50 = \mathbf{25.0 \text{ m}^2}$$

problems.finalAnswer:
**Summary of results:**

**(a)** Let $x$ = base distance, $y$ = wall height. The constraint is:
$$x^2 + y^2 = 100$$

**(b)** Rate of descent of the ladder's top at $x = 6$ m:
$$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{x}{y}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt} = -\frac{6}{8}(0.4) = -0.300 \text{ m/s}$$

**(c)** Rate of change of triangle area at $x = 6$ m:
$$\frac{dA}{dt} = 0.700 \text{ m}^2\text{/s}$$

Maximum area (achieved at $x = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07$ m):
$$A_{\max} = 25.0 \text{ m}^2$$

verdict.rederivation: x² + y² = 100; dy/dt = −0.3; the area A = ½xy is maximized at x = 5√2 → 25 m². An excellent multi-part problem — related rates AND optimization in one.
